title: Locusts, Fire, a Plumb Line, and a Priest
summary: Amos sees three visions. Twice, when God shows him locusts and then fire consuming the land, Amos pleads for Jacob and the LORD relents. The third time God shows a plumb line and declares he will no longer spare Israel. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reports Amos to King Jeroboam and orders him back to Judah; Amos answers that he was a herdsman whom the LORD called, and he pronounces judgment on Amaziah.
story: The book of Amos now shifts from speeches to visions. Chapters 7 to 9 contain five visions, and this chapter holds the first three, with a story inserted between the third and the fourth. Up to now Amos has argued Israel's guilt from every side. Here the reader sees the prophet interceding for the people he has been condemning, and then sees the moment when intercession ends. The narrative of Amos and Amaziah shows why: the nation's official religion has told the prophet to be quiet. It is the only story about Amos's life in the whole book, and it explains how a Judean farmer came to preach at the royal shrine of Israel.
historical:
Bethel, about eleven miles north of Jerusalem, had been one of the two royal sanctuaries of the northern kingdom since Jeroboam I set up a golden calf there after the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:28-33), around 930 BC. Amaziah calls it "the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom" (verse 13): a state shrine, where the priest served at the king's pleasure. The king in this chapter is Jeroboam II (about 793 to 753 BC).

Amos's words in verse 9 were against "the house of Jeroboam", his dynasty. Amaziah's report in verse 11 sharpens it to "Jeroboam will die by the sword", which Amos had not said. As it happened, Jeroboam II died a natural death (2 Kings 14:29), but his son Zechariah reigned only six months before he was assassinated by Shallum (2 Kings 15:8-10), ending the dynasty by the sword as Amos had warned. Within about thirty years of Jeroboam's death, Assyria had taken Samaria and sent Israel into exile.
cultural:
The "king's harvest" in verse 1 probably refers to the first cutting of hay or grain taken as tax for the royal stables, after which the late spring crop was what the farmers had left to live on. Locusts at that moment would leave the people with nothing. The fire that "consumed the great deep" (verse 4) pictures a drought or heat so intense that it seems to dry up the waters beneath the earth, the deep (tehom) of Genesis 1:2.

A plumb line is a weight on a cord used by builders to check whether a wall is vertical. A wall out of plumb must be pulled down. Amos describes himself as a herdsman and "a tender of sycamore-fig trees" (verse 14). The sycamore fig produced a cheap fruit eaten by the poor; growers slit or pinched the young fruit to help it ripen. Since sycamore figs grow in warmer lowlands rather than in the hills of Tekoa, Amos may have owned or worked land elsewhere, a sign that he was a man of some means, not necessarily a poor laborer. "Son of a prophet" means a member of a prophetic guild, like the "sons of the prophets" who gathered around Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2).
literary: The first two visions follow an identical pattern: God shows, Amos intercedes, God relents with a short "It will not happen". The repetition sets up the third vision, where the pattern breaks. God asks, "Amos, what do you see?", Amos answers, and God explains, but this time Amos does not pray and God does not relent. The fourth vision (8:1-3) will follow the same question-and-answer form. Between them stands a prose narrative (verses 10 to 17) that is linked to the third vision by its closing words about the house of Jeroboam and the sword. The narrative is itself built as a confrontation: Amaziah speaks to the king, then to Amos; Amos answers with his own call and then a word of judgment that turns Amaziah's accusation ("Israel will surely go into exile") into Amos's final line.

outline.t: First vision: locusts, and the LORD relents
Second vision: fire, and the LORD relents
Third vision: the plumb line, no longer spared
Amaziah reports Amos and orders him out of Bethel
Amos's call and his word against Amaziah

doctrines.note: Amos's intercession changes what happens: twice the LORD relents in answer to his plea. Scripture presents prayer as genuinely heard by God and effective, while also showing, in the third vision, that there comes a point when judgment will proceed.

Amos insists that his authority came from God's call, not from training or office: "the LORD took me from following the flock" (verse 15). The official priest tries to silence the word, but God's word does not depend on institutional permission.
The plumb line shows that God measures his people by a true standard. Judgment is not arbitrary; it is the recognition that the wall is no longer straight.

words.note: Anakh, traditionally plumb line. The word occurs only in this passage in the Hebrew Bible, four times. Because a related Akkadian word means tin, some scholars suggest the vision is of tin (perhaps tin for weapons, or a wall of tin, a pun on a Hebrew word for groaning). The traditional reading, a builder's plumb line testing a wall, remains the most common, and either way the vision announces that Israel has failed God's test.

Nacham, to relent or be sorry. When used of God it describes him turning from a threatened action, often in response to prayer or repentance (Exodus 32:14, Jonah 3:10). The word does not mean God was mistaken; it shows that his threats are real warnings within a relationship, not fixed fate.

Navi, prophet. Amos says he was "not a prophet", which may mean he was not a professional prophet earning his bread by it, as Amaziah implied. The Hebrew has no verb, so it can be read "I am not a prophet" or "I was not a prophet", and interpreters differ. Either way, Amos grounds his authority in the LORD's call, not in a guild.

christ: Amos standing between God and the people, pleading "How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?", belongs to a line of intercessors that includes Abraham and Moses. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one intercessor who does not stop, who lives always to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25). The confrontation with Amaziah also anticipates Jesus' own experience: he too was an outsider without official credentials, challenged by the leaders of the temple about his authority (Mark 11:27-33), and accused of speaking against the nation and its holy place. Like Amos, he answered by pointing to the authority of the one who sent him. These are patterns, not predictions.

hard.q: If God relents in answer to prayer, does God change his mind?
hard.a: The chapter says plainly that "the LORD relented from this plan" (verse 3), while other passages say God does not change his mind as humans do (Numbers 23:19, 1 Samuel 15:29). Readers have handled this in several ways. Many classical theologians hold that God's purposes are unchanging and that texts like this describe God's action from the human side: God has determined to answer the prayers he himself prompts. Others, including open theists, take the language more directly, arguing that God genuinely responds to human action in time. A middle view stresses that God's threats are conditional by nature (Jeremiah 18:7-10), so relenting is consistent with his unchanging character. All agree that the text wants readers to believe prayer matters to God.

questions: Amos pleads for Israel even while announcing its judgment. How does praying for people change the way you speak to them or about them?
Amaziah treats Bethel as the king's sanctuary. What happens to religion when it serves the interests of the powerful?
Amos was an ordinary worker called to speak for God. What does his story say about who God uses and what gives a message authority?
